statements.text: My legislation takes common-sense and long-overdue measures to protect consumers from harmful bias and discrimination resulting from the widespread use of automated systems that are governed by computer algorithms, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. [...] the very same automated technologies that are being misused and abused by social media companies are similarly being used without oversight by a wide range of industries to make critical, split-second decisions about people's health care, housing, finances, employment, and so much more. [...] these calculations are the products of systems designed by humans, subjecting them to a wide range of flaws that reinforce broader societal discrimination, particularly against women and people of color.
statements.context: US House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on legislation to protect online users, March 1, 2022.

statements.text: Furthermore, China's AI Plan for 2030 highlights the government's plan to become a leader in AI, which they believe is vital to their military and economic position in the world. [...] The Chinese government could easily take advantage of their continued work in this field and utilize it to directly harm U.S. interests.
statements.context: Written statement submitted for the record by Chairman Bennie G. Thompson at a House Homeland Security Subcommittee hearing on emerging technologies and security risks.

statements.text: Thank you. For years, I have been extremely concerned by the potential harms posed by deepfakes where AI-enabled synthetic images or recordings appear to be authentic, making it difficult for viewers to distinguish between reality and disinformation. To address this challenge, I have introduced the DEEPFAKES Accountability Act to implement criminal and civil penalties for malicious deepfakes, while directing DHS to establish a task force to prepare for the National security implications of deepfakes.
statements.context: US House hearing on emerging-technology security risks, questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: At the same time, there is concern that hackers will be able to exploit vulnerabilities in AI for nefarious purposes. [...] As deepfake technology becomes more sophisticated, experts anticipate that it will be used to further sow political tensions, disrupt public confidence in election outcomes, violate human rights, and facilitate criminal activity. [...] That is why I have introduced the DEEPFAKES Accountability Act to implement criminal and civil penalties for malicious deepfakes.
statements.context: Opening statement by Chairwoman Yvette D. Clarke at a House Homeland Security subcommittee hearing on emerging technologies and security risks.

statements.text: AI systems are often trained on the datasets that replicate human biases, and, thus, bias is built into the technology itself. [...] I am concerned that, without proper transparency and explicit steps to mitigate against bias, the use of artificial intelligence and critical decisions could erode essential civil rights protections in the digital realm.
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke speaking during a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on a national data privacy standard.

statements.text: Well, I've long been a champion for protecting vulnerable communities from the harms that come with new technologies, and that is why I wrote my Algorithmic Accountability Act to protect against built-in bias in automated critical decisions like algorithms and AI. [...] I agree, we need more guardrails in place on AI, which is why I introduced the Real Political Ads Act earlier this month and plan to reintroduce my Algorithmic Accountability Act and Deep Fakes Accountability Act this Congress.
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke speaks during a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on NTIA oversight, questioning an administration witness on AI policy coordination.

statements.text: What are AI companies currently doing to evaluate risks created by their systems before and after the systems are deployed?
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee hearing on AI and data innovation, during a period of legislative dysfunction in the House.

statements.text: It is essential for companies to evaluate and mitigate the potential risk of a system before it is released. [...] We needs strong rules that prevent companies from releasing systems that replicate and amplify the harmful biases in our society.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, where Rep. Yvette Clarke advocates for algorithmic accountability and questions a witness about impact assessments.

statements.text: Administrator Davidson, in your opinion, why is it important to ensure that there is accountability in how AI systems and algorithms are deployed and developed? And in what ways is NTIA working to foster accountability within the AI ecosystem?
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke questions NTIA Administrator Alan Davidson during an oversight hearing on the agency's AI accountability efforts.

statements.text: What do you see as the most relevant cyber threats presented by AI? And, conversely, how can cybersecurity professionals leverage AI tools to fend off cyber attacks?
statements.context: House committee hearing on cybersecurity in the digital era.

statements.text: AI systems are trained on datasets which often replicate human biases and thus, the bias is built into the very technology created to improve our lives and keep us safe. [...] For example, AI designed for law enforcement purposes that was trained on historic police or crime data may serve to reproduce or expand existing inequities in policing as those are not an accurate reflection of crime but rather of police activity and crime reporting, which can be fraught with bias.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House committee hearing on AI and homeland security.

statements.text: Developers and deployers of artificial intelligence, whether in the realm of securing the homeland or providing a service to consumers must be thoughtful and intentional in the creation and rollout of this technology.
statements.context: Opening statement and question during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on AI in homeland defense.

statements.text: Facial recognition technology is yet another tool powered by artificial intelligence which has the serious potential for harm and bias, particularly for communities of color. The collection and use of biometric information in any instance, but particularly with respect to AI tools, is fraught with the potential for harmful outcomes and must be subject to rigorous oversight.
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke questions FTC Chair Lina Khan during a House Appropriations subcommittee hearing on the FTC's FY2025 budget.

statements.text: Under the leadership of Chair Khan, the FTC has taken important steps to combat unsolicited robocalls, scams turbocharged by AI tools [...] I am concerned about our lack of Federal data privacy standards and the ability for unchecked automated critical decisionmaking processes like algorithms to [...] produce biased or discriminatory outcomes [...] the FTC has taken steps, important steps, to addressing potential algorithmic discrimination, including through its commercial surveillance rulemaking. Chair Khan, what do you see as the Commission's current role in addressing algorithmic discrimination, and what kind of authority might the Commission need in the future to stay ahead of advancements in technology?
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke questions FTC Chair Lina Khan during a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on the FTC's FY2025 budget.

statements.text: Facial recognition technology is a clear example of a tool powered by AI that time and time again has been prone to unjustified bias, particularly against members of communities of color.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on online harms, addressing FTC enforcement against biased AI and the impact of firing Democratic commissioners.

statements.text: those terminations included hundreds of newer hires from the Center for Device and Radiological Health, or CDRH, who had been recruited because of their expertise in artificial intelligence and other technological fields that support a review of medical devices.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Energy and Commerce Oversight subcommittee hearing on medical-device cybersecurity.

statements.text: My top priority with respect to the growing use of AI is simple. [...] Americans do not forfeit their civil liberties when they go online.
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce Committee hearing on AI technology and American competitiveness, April 9, 2025.

statements.text: A 10-year moratorium seems wildly irresponsible given the rapid pace of technological advancement, especially in the field of artificial intelligence.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership.

statements.text: So let me be clear. I say this is a giveaway to Big Tech at the expense of Americans' personal freedom, privacy, and safety online. [...] there will be no recourse or guardrails in more than half of the States that have responded quickly to their residents' concerns about the risks posed by AI.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI applications in communications and technology.

statements.text: Ensuring that we have proper safeguards in place for sophisticated AI systems is only one piece of the puzzle. It is also critically important that consumers understand the abilities and shortcomings of AI systems that are poised to become an increasing part of our everyday lives.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee hearing on AI applications in communications and technology.

statements.text: The Republican AI moratorium in the House's version of the reconciliation bill would prohibit New York City and New York State from adopting and enforcing laws governing AVs, stripping the city and the State of their oversight of AV deployment on New York roads, making AV deployment that much less safe in New York.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House Commerce Subcommittee hearing on NHTSA and motor vehicle safety.

statements.text: Ms. Chase, how would an AI moratorium that ends State programs to test and provide guardrails for AVs deployment impact industry growth and adoption?
statements.context: House Oversight committee hearing on NHTSA and motor vehicle safety, questioning a witness about AV regulation.

statements.text: A new term has been coined, “AI psychosis,” which describes when a user’s interactions with a chatbot lead to distorted beliefs or even delusions. [...] As we’ve seen in some absolutely tragic cases, users experiencing mental health crises have even taken their own lives after extensive communication with these chatbots.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee hearing on AI chatbot risks and benefits.

statements.text: I have recently introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act and have worked in the past on bills related to the harms caused by deepfake technologies.
statements.context: US congressional hearing titled 'Innovation with Integrity: Examining the Risks and Benefits of AI Chatbots'; Rep. Clarke delivers opening remarks before questioning the panel.

statements.text: And that is why they continue to entertain the idea of a moratorium on State AI laws, even after it was defeated 99 to 1 in the Senate. In 2025 alone, all 50 States introduced legislation on AI, while Republicans in Congress offered no Federal alternative other than preemption. It is no mistake that the only Republican proposal frees AI and Big Tech companies from all oversight.
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke delivers opening remarks at a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on legislative solutions to protect children and teens online.

statements.text: It does not matter if it is a natural virus or a virus created by AI.
statements.context: Ranking Member Yvette Clarke's opening statement at a House Energy and Commerce Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee hearing on biosecurity and AI.

statements.text: Can you please identify the consequences we have seen in AI innovation and workforce development due to the fact that the President has disbanded Natcast, erasing its existing research and development workforce efforts and sought to rewrite existing and pending agreements with CHIPS recipients?
statements.context: Rep. Yvette Clarke questions a witness at a House hearing on the semiconductor ecosystem.

statements.text: How can this administration plausibly claim that they want to onshore chip production, unleash AI development, and spur workforce development when they are actively putting up unnecessary hurdles?
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Yvette Clarke at a House subcommittee hearing on the semiconductor ecosystem and computing power.
